questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state that a halving search needs the range ordered by the same comparison the search itself uses
questions.stem: A halving search looks up a Part by its part number, and the array is sorted ascending by part number. Which precondition does the search rely on?

options.text: The range is ordered ascending by the very key the search compares at each step
The range is ordered by name, since any ordering at all makes halving legal
options.misconception: an ordering by some other field is good enough to halve

options.text: The range holds no duplicate keys, or the midpoint arithmetic becomes invalid
options.misconception: duplicate keys break the arithmetic of a halving search

options.text: The range was built by insertion sort rather than by any other sort routine
options.misconception: only one particular sort can produce a searchable range

questions.explanation: Halving is justified by the claim that everything left of the midpoint sorts before the key and everything right of it sorts after, and that claim only follows if the array is ordered by the key the search is comparing. The tempting answer accepts any ordering, but ordering by name proves nothing about part numbers, so the discarded half may well hold the match. The sort routine used is irrelevant; only the relationship between the order and the compared key matters.
questions.hint: Ask what the discarded half would need to be true about the key.

questions.learningObjective: state that a failed exhaustive scan costs one element comparison per element regardless of where the key would have been
questions.stem: An exhaustive linear scan runs for every index of a nine element array and the key is not present. How many element comparisons does it make?

options.text: Nine, because a failed scan has to compare the key with all nine entries
None, because a scan that finds nothing makes no comparisons at all
options.misconception: an unsuccessful search somehow skips its comparisons

options.text: One, because the scan stops at the first entry that fails to match
options.misconception: the first mismatch ends an exhaustive scan

options.text: Five, because the middle entry is reached before the scan can give up
options.misconception: a failed scan can stop once it passes the middle

questions.explanation: A scan that never stops early has no evidence to stop on, since every entry it has seen is simply not the key, so it visits all nine and compares nine times. The tempting answers imagine an early exit that the code has no rule for, and an early exit after a mismatch is only sound on ordered data. This is why the failed case has a fixed cost while the successful case varies with where the key sits.
questions.hint: Ask what would make the loop stop before the last index.

questions.learningObjective: relate the number of insertion sort shifts to the number of inversions in the input
questions.stem: An insertion sort shifts an element one slot right for every earlier element that is larger than it. What determines the total number of shifts?

options.text: The number of inverted pairs, one shift for each value that must pass another
The number of distinct values, since equal values never need to move at all
options.misconception: the shift count is the size of the value set

options.text: One shift per outer pass, because each pass opens exactly one gap
options.misconception: each pass opens one gap and therefore shifts once

options.text: The number of already sorted prefixes, since each one adds a single pass
options.misconception: sorted prefixes are what the shift counter measures

questions.explanation: Each shift moves one value past one larger predecessor, so the count of shifts is exactly the count of inverted pairs and nothing else drives it. The tempting answers attach the count to the shape of the value set or to the number of passes, but a fully reversed run of n values has an inversion for every pair, which is why the worst case grows with the square of n. Nearly ordered input has few inversions, and that is what makes insertion sort cheap on it.
questions.hint: Ask which single element moves for each pair that is out of order.

questions.learningObjective: identify the ordering precondition that an early exit in a linear scan introduces

Nothing, since a larger entry rules the key out in any arrangement of values
options.misconception: one larger entry rules out a later match without any order

options.text: A duplicate free range, or a larger entry could sit beside a matching one
options.misconception: a larger neighbour makes a match impossible in the same slot

options.text: A descending order, since a larger entry is what the scan must meet first
options.misconception: the early exit needs the data turned upside down

The tempting answer reads a larger entry as a local fact rather than a global one, and on shuffled data a key can sit happily two slots after a bigger number. The cheap early exit is exactly the thing that buys its speed with a precondition.

questions.learningObjective: hand trace the midpoint sequence and final index of a halving search
questions.stem: Trace this search: class Trace1 { static String find(int[] a, int key) { int lo = 0; int hi = a.length - 1; StringBuilder t = new StringBuilder(); while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; t.append(mid).append(' '); if (a[mid] == key) { return t.toString().trim() + " -> " + mid; } if (a[mid] < key) { lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid - 1; } } return t.toString().trim() + " -> -1"; } } int[] data = {2, 5, 8, 12, 14, 20, 27}; System.out.print(Trace1.find(data, 14)); What is printed?

options.misconception: the search stops as soon as the range is small enough to hold one entry
the second midpoint is taken from the untouched right half
the range is halved from the low end regardless of the comparison

questions.explanation: The midpoint of indices 0 through 6 is 3 holding 12, which is too small, so lo moves to 4; the next midpoint of 4 through 6 is 5 holding 20, which is too large, so hi moves to 4; and the midpoint of 4 through 4 is the match itself. The tempting answer stops one step early, but the range still held a candidate after 5, and a search that returns as soon as the range looks small abandons the entry it was sent to find. Each recorded number is a midpoint that was actually compared.
questions.hint: Recompute lo plus half of hi minus lo after every update.

the final midpoint is reported even though the key is absent
the second midpoint comes from the middle of the whole array

options.misconception: the early exit should compare for a smaller entry instead

options.text: the scan misses the match because the array must be copied before it is read
options.misconception: a search needs its own copy of the array first

options.text: the scan misses the match because index three is past the end of a four entry array
options.misconception: the last index of an array cannot be reached by a scan

questions.explanation: The first entry is 9, which is larger than 6, so the early exit breaks before the cursor ever reaches index 3 and the match is never examined. The tempting answers blame the direction of the comparison or the length of the array, but both are fine and the defect is the precondition the early exit quietly assumed. A break on a larger entry is only justified when the range is ordered, and here 6 was sitting in plain sight two slots further along.
questions.hint: Ask what the code believes about entries it has not visited yet.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a halving search run over a range that was only partly ordered
questions.stem: A clerk runs int[] data = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 0, 4, 6, 8}; java.util.Arrays.sort(data, 0, 5); and then a halving search for key 6 over the whole array reports -1, though 6 sits at index 7. What is the fault?

options.text: only the first five slots are ordered, so halving the whole range discards a real match
the sort must cover the whole array before any halving search is sound
options.misconception: ordering only the part that is searched is enough

options.text: the search must start at index one because index zero is never a candidate
options.misconception: the first slot of a range is never eligible for a match

options.text: the key must be sorted into the array before the search can compare it
options.misconception: a search compares by sorting the key into place

questions.explanation: Sorting the first five slots orders only the front of the range, so when the midpoint lands on 9 the method discards everything to its right, and 6 is sitting in that discarded region. The tempting answer asks for a full sort, but the real fault is the mismatch between the range that was ordered and the range that was searched. Halving needs the whole range it walks to be ordered, not a prefix of it.
questions.hint: Compare the span that was sorted with the span the search walks.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a halving search whose update directions do not match the data order
questions.stem: A clerk runs int[] data = {88, 76, 61, 54, 43, 30}; int key = 54; with a halving loop that treats a larger midpoint as the reason to move lo up, and the search reports -1 though 54 sits at index 3. What is the fault?

options.text: the halves are swapped for this order, so the search discards the side holding the key
the midpoint must come from the length rather than from the two ends
options.misconception: a midpoint cannot be computed from the range ends

options.text: the key must be doubled so that it matches the descending spacing
options.misconception: descending data requires a transformed key

options.text: the search must visit the high half first because the data descends
options.misconception: a descending range obliges the search to start at the top

questions.explanation: In a descending range a larger midpoint means the key lies to the right, so moving lo up throws away the correct side, and the walk collapses to -1 while 54 waits at index 3. The tempting answers rearrange the loop or the key rather than the comparison, but the arithmetic of the midpoint is not what failed. Order decides which side is worth keeping, and a search that keeps the other one finds nothing no matter how well the midpoint is computed.
questions.hint: Ask which side of a larger entry holds the smaller values here.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an outer loop that spends a pass on the entry that is already sorted
questions.stem: A sort runs int[] data = {3, 1, 2}; for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) { int key = data[i]; int j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && data[j] > key) { data[j + 1] = data[j]; j--; } data[j + 1] = key; } and the array does come out as [1, 2, 3]. What is the fault?

options.text: the first pass is pure overhead, because one entry is already a sorted prefix
the loop must stop one slot early or the final entry is never placed
options.misconception: the outer bound excludes the entry that needs sorting

options.text: the loop writes the key into index zero and so destroys the first entry
options.misconception: the key is always deposited at the front of the array

options.text: the loop needs a key variable or the first entry is read after it changes
options.misconception: the key may only be read into a local before the loop

questions.explanation: At i equal to 0 the cursor starts one below the array, the guard fails at once, and the single entry is written back to where it came from, so a whole pass is spent doing nothing. The tempting answers predict corruption or a lost entry, but the first pass is harmless because a one entry prefix is already sorted, which is exactly why the correct loop starts at one. The output looks right and the cost is one wasted pass per call, the kind of defect that survives testing.
questions.hint: Ask what the while guard can possibly do when j is already below zero.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the two midpoint formulas and the overflow the naive one produces
questions.stem: Trace this helper: class Mid1 { static String both(int lo, int hi) { return (lo + hi) / 2 + " " + (lo + (hi - lo) / 2); } } System.out.print(Mid1.both(1_500_000_000, 1_600_000_000)); What is printed?

options.misconception: a large index sum simply cannot overflow an int
the shifted form is the one that loses the high bits
the naive form is safe and the shifted form overflows

questions.explanation: The two ends sum to 3_100_000_000, which is past the largest int, so the sum wraps to a negative number and the halving yields -597483648, while the shifted form keeps the ends apart and reports the correct 1_550_000_000. The tempting answer says the overflow cannot happen, but any range whose two ends are both large is exactly where it does. The shifted formula costs one extra subtraction and removes the hazard entirely, which is why it is the one worth remembering.
questions.hint: Decide which of the two additions can exceed the largest int.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a halving search that compares objects by their ordering rather than their identity
questions.stem: Trace this search: class Trace9 { static int find(String[] a, String key) { int lo = 0; int hi = a.length - 1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; int c = a[mid].compareTo(key); if (c == 0) { return mid; } if (c < 0) { lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid - 1; } } return -1; } } String[] words = {"ant", "bee", "cat", "dog", "emu"}; System.out.print(Trace9.find(words, new String("cat"))); What is printed?

options.misconception: a search needs the very same object, not an equal one
the ordered comparison finds the entry just before the key
the midpoint of five entries is computed as index zero

questions.explanation: The key is a separately built String, so a reference test would have failed, but compareTo reports zero for cat against cat and the midpoint of five entries is index 2, so the search prints 2. The tempting answer insists on identity, which is a different question from ordering and is not what an ordered array is built on. Once the range is sorted by the ordering the search uses, any equal element is a legitimate hit, however it was constructed.
questions.hint: Ask which comparison the method makes instead of a reference test.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: supply the update that keeps a halving search returning the first matching slot
questions.stem: A clerk wants the first slot holding the key rather than whichever slot the midpoint lands on. int[] data = {4, 4, 4, 7}; int key = 4; int lo = 0; int hi = data.length - 1; int first = -1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if (data[mid] == key) { first = mid; ____ } else if (data[mid] < key) { lo = mid + 1; } else { hi = mid - 1; } } System.out.print(first); Which fragment fills the blank so the program prints 0?

options.text: hi = mid - 1;
lo = mid + 1;
options.misconception: keeping the equal side on the right finds the first match

options.text: hi = mid;
options.misconception: the upper end may stop at the midpoint it just matched

options.text: hi = mid - 2;
options.misconception: the upper end must drop below the midpoint by a whole step

questions.explanation: Recording the match and then dropping the upper end to one below the midpoint keeps walking left through the run of equal entries, so 2, then 0, is recorded and the walk ends with 0. The tempting fragment keeps the equal side on the right, which walks to the last equal entry instead, and the version that stops at mid never shrinks the range on a match. Finding a run's start is not the default behaviour and has to be built in by choice of direction.
questions.hint: Ask which side of a matching midpoint could still contain an earlier match.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: supply the update that lets two halving walks bracket a run of equal entries
questions.stem: A clerk counts how many entries equal a key by bracketing the run with two halving walks. int[] data = {3, 5, 5, 5, 8}; int key = 5; int lo = 0; int hi = data.length - 1; int left = -1; int right = -1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if (data[mid] < key) { lo = mid + 1; } else { left = mid; hi = mid - 1; } } lo = 0; hi = data.length - 1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if (data[mid] <= key) { ____ } else { right = mid - 1; } } System.out.print(right - left + 1); Which fragment fills the blank so the program prints 3?

options.text: lo = mid + 1;
hi = mid - 1;
options.misconception: the second walk should also settle towards the low end

options.text: hi = mid;
options.misconception: the upper end may rest on the midpoint it just accepted

options.text: lo = mid + 1; left = mid;
options.misconception: the second walk may also record the run's first slot

questions.explanation: The first walk already pinned the run's start at 1, and the second must push past every entry that is not larger than the key, so the range climbs to 4, meets 8, records right as 3 and finishes, giving a run of 3. The tempting fragment shrinks the wrong end and leaves right at -1, and the last one overwrites the run's start with a later match so the subtraction is wrong. Bracketing a run means one walk that only moves up and another that only moves down, with each storing the edge it lands on.
questions.hint: Ask which way the range has to move while every entry is still at or below the key.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which claims about comparison and shift counts are true
questions.stem: Consider int[] data = {5, 1, 4, 2, 3}. Which claims about searching and sorting that array are true?

options.text: Insertion sort makes six shifts, which is the number of inverted pairs in the array
An exhaustive scan for a key that is absent makes five element comparisons
A halving search can need five comparisons in the worst case, the same as a scan
options.misconception: halving still costs one comparison per entry at worst

options.text: Insertion sort makes no shifts at all on an array that is already ordered
A scan that stops on the first match always makes one comparison, wherever the key sits
options.misconception: an early exit costs a single comparison regardless of position

questions.explanation: A, B and D all follow from the two rules at work, shifts equal inversions and a scan that cannot stop early visits every entry. C is the belief that halving gives no worst case advantage, but five entries need at most three midpoints before the range empties. E confuses an early exit with a free search, since the key at the last slot still costs a comparison for every entry before it.
questions.hint: Ask of each claim whether it follows from the number of entries or from the number of out of order pairs.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which conditions are genuine preconditions of the search and sort routines
questions.stem: Four routines are described below. Which of the stated conditions are genuine preconditions of the routine named?

options.text: A halving search needs the whole range ordered by the key it compares
A linear scan that stops at the first larger entry needs the range ordered
An exhaustive linear scan needs no order, only a key comparable to each entry
A halving search needs a range free of duplicate keys, or the midpoint breaks
options.misconception: duplicate keys make a halving search unsound

options.text: Insertion sort needs input that is already ordered, so each key lands without shifting
options.misconception: insertion sort is a repair step for ordered data

questions.explanation: A, B and C name conditions the routines genuinely rely on, two of them about ordering and one about comparability alone. D is wrong because repeated keys only make the returned index less specific, not the search unsound, since the midpoint test and both updates still hold. E reverses the picture entirely, since ordered input is the one case where insertion sort does the least work and disordered input is exactly what it is built to fix.
questions.hint: For each claim, ask whether breaking the condition would actually break the routine.
